candidates.attacker_control: The attacker fully controls the bearer token string that the application passes to `JWTDecoder.decode`: the base64url header (including `alg` = `none` and, in the map overload, `kid`), the base64url payload (arbitrary claims such as `sub`, `iss`, `exp`, roles), and the trailing dot that makes it a two-segment token. No key material is needed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the correct-behavior paths: three-part tokens with `alg: none` and supplied verifiers ARE rejected (line 159, MissingVerifierException), so the bypass requires the two-segment trailing-dot form; a two-part token whose algorithm a supplied verifier supports (e.g. HS256 with an HMACVerifier) IS rejected (line 164, InvalidJWTSignatureException) — confirming the author intended to reject missing signatures and that the failure is specific to the `verifier == null` selection result. Verified that HMACVerifier/RSAVerifier cannot return true for `none`, that no `none` verifier exists in the snapshot (only UnsecuredSigner, which is encoder-side), and that Algorithm's enum constant is exactly `none` (matching Jackson's case-sensitive enum binding), so the header parses as intended. No test files or in-repo callers exist in the snapshot, so no application-side countermeasure could be examined; README lines 5-6 claim a prior JWT-validation CVE (2018-1000125) was fixed in >= 1.3.0 and pom.xml declares 1.3.0, which may mean this is a residual/incomplete fix rather than the same issue — that remains unverified from source alone. No runtime execution, no external lookups.
candidates.impact: Signature verification is bypassed: an attacker can fabricate arbitrary claims (identity, roles, issuer, expiry) and have them returned as a validly decoded JWT by any application using the documented decode-with-verifier API. In practice this yields authentication and authorization bypass for services protecting resources with JWTs from this library. The attacker needs no secret or signing key. A related consequence of the same unverified path is that claim-time validation semantics of the intent comments are not applied to the accepted token.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application validates tokens with this library and passes at least one Verifier (either `decode(encodedJWT, verifier...)` or `decode(encodedJWT, mapOfVerifiers)`), as in the README examples. 2) The application treats a returned JWT as signature-verified (it has no way to tell from the returned object that no signature was checked). 3) The attacker can supply the token value (standard bearer-token/cookie threat model). For the array overload the header must carry `alg: none` (or any algorithm unsupported by the supplied verifiers, e.g. RS256 token when only an HMAC verifier is configured); for the map overload an unknown/absent `kid` alone is sufficient. `exp`/`nbf` may be set in the future so the two remaining claim checks pass.
candidates.root_cause: In `JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...)`, the two-part/no-signature handling at lines 70-76 is entered only when `verifiers.length == 0`. When verifiers ARE supplied, verifier selection (lines 79-84) leaves `verifier == null` for a header algorithm no supplied verifier supports — which is always the case for `Algorithm.none`, since HMACVerifier supports only HS* and RSAVerifier only RS*. The private `decode` then rejects an unsigned token only if a matching verifier was found (`parts.length == 2 && verifier != null`, line 164) and only requires a verifier for the three-part form (line 159). For a two-part token with `verifier == null`, both guards are false, the verification block at lines 168-172 is skipped, and the payload is deserialized and returned (lines 174-186). The same hole exists in the map-based overload (lines 125-142): an absent/unknown `kid` or an `alg` no map verifier supports yields `verifier == null`, again falling through to an unverified decode. This contradicts the in-source intent comments at line 69 ('if no verifiers were provided, decode if header says none, else throw an exception') and lines 163-164 ('A verifier was provided but no signature exists, this is treated as an invalid signature').
candidates.title: Unsigned `alg: none` JWT is accepted even when verifiers are supplied (signature verification bypass)
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker token = base64url('{"alg":"none"}') + '.' + base64url('{"sub":"attacker","exp":<future>}') + '.' (two segments plus trailing dot). 2) `getParts` (189-197) accepts it: `split("\\.")` yields 2 elements and `encodedJWT.endsWith(".")` is true. 3) Header deserializes; `header.algorithm == Algorithm.none` (Algorithm.java line 58; Header.algorithm is a plain `@JsonProperty("alg")` field). 4) The guard at line 70 (`parts.length == 2 && verifiers.length == 0`) is false because the caller supplied verifiers, so the request is NOT rejected here. 5) The selection loop (79-84) calls `canVerify(none)`; HMACVerifier (55-65) and RSAVerifier (60-70) return false for `none`, so `verifier` remains `null`. 6) `decode(encodedJWT, header, parts, null)` (line 86): line 159 requires `parts.length == 3` (false), line 164 requires `verifier != null` (false), and the `parts.length == 3` verification block (168-172) is skipped, so `verifier.verify(...)` is never invoked. 7) The payload is base64-decoded and deserialized at line 174; `isExpired()`/`isUnavailableForProcessing()` can be satisfied by attacker-chosen future timestamps; the JWT is returned as if verified. 8) Map overload (117-143): with a non-empty map, `keyFunction` returns `header.get("kid")`; if the attacker omits `kid` or uses an unknown value, `verifiers.get(key)` is null, `canVerify` is never called, and the identical unverified 2-segment decode path executes. The relation index corroborates the structure (indexed call edges: public decode -> private decode at lines 86 and 142; `Verifier.verify` invoked only from line 171 inside the three-part branch), but it is navigation-only and not proof of runtime behavior.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: the snapshot contains no tests or callers, so the integration predicate (application passes verifiers and trusts the result) is assumed from the README's documented usage, not observed. The exact upstream fix history and the relationship to the README's CVE-2018-1000125 notice were not verified against any external source. The map-overload variant's `kid`-miss trigger is reasoned from source but was not executed.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347), leading to authentication bypass (CWE-287)

coverage_summary: All 35 files in the assigned snapshot were accounted for: 32 Java source files under src/main/java/org/primeframework/jwt (every one read in full), plus pom.xml, README.md and .gitignore. The P1 relation index reports 35/35 source files indexed with no omissions or hash mismatches (188 symbols, 399 calls, 258 edges; 1 fact), so index coverage is complete for this tree; however, it is syntactic navigation only — no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability claims derive from it, and each indexed edge used (public->private decode, Verifier.verify call site) was re-verified in source text. No test sources, no in-repo callers, and no resources/config files exist in the snapshot, so findings rest on library semantics, the README's documented usage, and the in-code intent comments.
limitations: No code was executed and no tests exist in the snapshot, so no runtime confirmation of the bypass or of any application integration was possible.
The security impact depends on how a consuming application uses the decoded JWT; no consuming code is present in the snapshot, so impact is argued from the library's public API and README examples.
The relation index supplies only syntactic calls/containment; no complete data flow, reachability, or exploitability proof, and unparsed/unsupported constructs (if any) would not appear.

The README's security notice about CVE-2018-1000125 and version 1.3.0 is repository-provided untrusted text; no external advisory, patch, or upstream comparison was consulted, so whether the observed behavior is an incomplete fix of that CVE or a distinct latent flaw is unverified.
Non-Java files were only skimmed for build/dependency context (Jackson 2.8.1, TestNG declared with no tests present); no dependency-level vulnerability analysis was performed.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsecured early-return paths (`decode` lines 70-76 and 125-131) return the payload without running `jwt.isExpired()` / `jwt.isUnavailableForProcessing()`, contrary to the method Javadoc that says expired/not-yet-valid JWTs are rejected. Only reachable when the caller provides NO verifiers (explicitly unsecured mode), and it is in the same code region as the primary finding; mentioned rather than submitted as a second candidate.
rejected_leads.reason: Real inconsistency, but requires the caller to have opted out of verification entirely (unsecured mode), so the security impact and evidence are weaker than the submitted bypass. Not split out per the one-candidate rule.

rejected_leads.lead: HMACVerifier.verify uses `Arrays.equals(signature, actualSignature)` (line 78), a non-constant-time MAC comparison (CWE-208).
rejected_leads.reason: Theoretical timing side channel; remote exploitation against an HMAC comparison is not established from source alone, and no evidence of an exploitable oracle exists in this library. Rejected as a finding.

rejected_leads.lead: A header without an `alg` member leaves `header.algorithm == null`; `canVerify(null)` performs a switch on a null enum in HMACVerifier/RSAVerifier (lines 56-57 / 61-62), throwing an uncaught NullPointerException instead of InvalidJWTException.
rejected_leads.reason: Availability/robustness issue, not a signature-verification bypass; impact is limited to exception type/DoS depending on caller handling. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: `getParts` accepts a token ending in `.` as a three-segment token (`h.p.s.`), and `lastIndexOf(".")` then makes the verified message `h.p.s` instead of `h.p.s.`.
rejected_leads.reason: Malformed-token parsing quirk; forging would still require a MAC/RSA signature valid over the shifted message, so no verification bypass was found. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: `JWT.getLong/getInteger/getBoolean/getList/getString` cast or parse attacker-chosen claim values (e.g. `(Long) object`, `Integer.parseInt`, unchecked `(List<String>) cast`), which can throw ClassCastException/NumberFormatException on crafted claims.
rejected_leads.reason: Caller-dependent robustness/DoS concern with no demonstrated security boundary crossing in this codebase; not competitive with the primary candidate. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: RSAUtils imports `sun.security.util.*` / `sun.security.x509.*` internal APIs and PEM parsing uses string `contains`/`indexOf` slicing.
rejected_leads.reason: Portability/maintenance concerns; no attacker-controlled key material enters these helpers in the documented API (verifier/signer keys are supplied by the application). No concrete security impact established. Rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: Public Javadoc for `decode(String, Verifier...)` says the FIRST verifier supporting the algorithm is used, but the loop (lines 80-84) does not break and the LAST matching verifier wins.
rejected_leads.reason: Documentation/behavior mismatch with no established security impact (all supplied verifiers are held to the same algorithm family); rejected as a standalone finding.

summary: Reviewed the 35-file prime-jwt 1.3.0 snapshot (32 Java files + pom.xml + README.md + .gitignore); every Java file was read, focusing on JWTDecoder/JWTEncoder, HMAC/RSA signer-verifier pairs, key/PEM handling, JSON mapping, and claim processing. Strongest candidate: JWTDecoder accepts an unsigned, two-segment JWT whose header says `alg: none` even when the caller supplied verifiers, so signature verification is silently skipped and the attacker-controlled payload is returned as a decoded/trusted JWT. The defect is the interaction of (a) verifier selection yielding `null` for algorithms no supplied verifier supports, and (b) the private `decode` only rejecting the missing-signature case when `verifier != null`. This contradicts the method's own intent comments and enables authentication/authorization bypass in the library's documented usage (`decode(encodedJWT, verifier)`).
